turns.content:
hey, so i was going through the open enrollment stuff during lunch and i'm looking at the wellness credit thing... $25/month, so $300/year, not nothing. the intranet banner says 'deadline oct 31' which had me thinking i'd need to move my physical up, but then i checked section 4.2 in the handbook. let me just paste it exactly:

"Section 4.2: The Health Risk Assessment questionnaire must be finalized in the portal by October 31. Biometric screening results from an in-network provider or on-site screening event may be submitted via physician attestation form through December 1 for discount application starting January 1."

so it looks like the questionnaire has to be done by oct 31, but the biometric stuff can come in later, up to dec 1? i already have my annual physical with dr. chen on november 14—that's my regular pcp, been seeing her for years. so if i read this right, i can knock out the online assessment before halloween and then just have dr. chen's office submit the screening results after my appointment in november, as long as it's before december 1. does that check out? just want to make sure i'm reading it right before i put it on the calendar.

Your reading matches the text you pasted. Section 4.2 sets two separate deadlines: the questionnaire by October 31, and biometric results by December 1. A November 14 physical falls inside the second window.

What the pasted text establishes:
- Health Risk Assessment: finalized in the portal by October 31.
- Biometric screening: results from an in-network provider (or on-site event) submitted via physician attestation form through December 1.
- Discount applies starting January 1.

What it does not establish, and what would settle each:
1. Whether Dr. Chen is in-network under the plan the wellness credit is tied to. Years of seeing her is not evidence of network status for this year's plan. Check: the plan's provider directory or the benefits portal.
2. Which biometric values the attestation form requires (commonly blood pressure, BMI or waist, glucose, cholesterol; some forms require fasting labs). If Dr. Chen's office needs lab results in hand to complete the form, a November 14 visit leaves about 2.5 weeks for labs to return and the form to be submitted. Check: download the attestation form now and bring it to the appointment.
3. Whether "submitted through December 1" means received by the plan by December 1 or postmarked/faxed by that date, and who submits (you or the provider). Check: the form instructions or HR.
4. Whether the October 31 banner also covers your enrollment election itself (choosing a plan, electing the wellness program). Section 4.2 covers the assessment only; if you must opt into the wellness program during open enrollment, that is likely an October 31 item too. Check: the open enrollment checklist.

Next action: complete the questionnaire before October 31; confirm Dr. Chen's network status and download the attestation form this week; bring the form to the November 14 visit and ask the office to complete it the same day if labs are not required, or set a target of November 24 for submission to leave margin before December 1.

yeah okay that all tracks. the network thing is a good point—i should probably just pull up the directory on the portal to make sure dr. chen's practice is still listed for this year. but the main thing i was worried about was whether the nov 14 physical would even work timing-wise, and it sounds like it does as long as i get the questionnaire done first.

so the attestation form... is that like a standard thing the doctor's office fills out, or is it a specific form from our benefits team that i need to bring with me? just trying to figure out if i should print something now or if dr. chen's office will have their own version.

Section 4.2 names a "physician attestation form" without specifying its source, so the text does not settle this. In practice, wellness programs almost always use their own form, not a generic one from the doctor's office.

What the pasted text supports: a specific document called a physician attestation form exists and is the required submission channel. It does not say where to get it.

What is typical, stated as inference from common program design rather than knowledge of your plan: the form is issued by the wellness vendor or benefits team, lists the exact biometric fields they will accept (e.g., blood pressure, height/weight or BMI, total cholesterol, HDL, glucose or A1c), requires the provider's signature and NPI or practice stamp, and often requires the screening date to fall within a defined window (for example, on or after a set date in the current year). A doctor's office usually does not have a version of this on hand; if you arrive without it, the office may give you a visit summary or lab printout, which many programs reject because the required signature and field format are missing.

Unknowns and how to resolve them:
1. Where the form lives. Check the wellness section of the benefits portal, usually under "forms" or "biometric screening"; if not there, email HR/benefits and ask for the "physician attestation form referenced in Section 4.2."
2. Whether it has a screening-date window. Read the form header before the appointment; a November 14 date almost certainly qualifies, but confirm.
3. Whether it requires fasting labs. If yes, ask Dr. Chen's office whether labs can be drawn before or at the November 14 visit so results are available for the form.
4. Submission method (portal upload, fax, mail) and whether you or the office submits. Read the form instructions.

Next action: locate and print the form this week, read the required fields and instructions, and call Dr. Chen's office before November 14 to tell them you will bring a wellness attestation form to be completed and signed at the visit.

ok so that makes sense, i'll grab the form from the portal before i go in. one more thing though—section 4.3 talks about "qualified biometric screening" and i'm wondering if the standard stuff dr. chen does at an annual physical counts. like fasting lipid panel, glucose, bp, bmi... is that usually what they want, or is there some specific panel or form they're looking for?

I do not have Section 4.3's text, so I cannot tell you what "qualified" means under your plan; if you paste it, I can check the list against what Dr. Chen does. The typical answer, stated as inference from common program design: the four items you named are the standard set most programs require.

Common "qualified biometric screening" components:
- Blood pressure (systolic/diastolic)
- Height and weight, reported as BMI; some programs also require waist circumference
- Total cholesterol, HDL, and often LDL and triglycerides (a fasting lipid panel covers all of these)
- Fasting glucose or A1c (some accept either, some require one specifically)
- Some programs add nicotine/cotinine or ask the provider to attest tobacco status

Where a standard physical can fall short:
1. The program requires a specific field the physical did not include (e.g., waist circumference, A1c rather than glucose, or a cotinine test). A routine physical often omits waist and cotinine.
2. The program defines "qualified" by who performs it or where: e.g., in-network provider, on-site event, or a contracted lab like Quest or LabCorp. The Section 4.2 text you pasted covers this ("in-network provider or on-site screening event"), so a Dr. Chen visit qualifies on that axis if she is in-network.
3. The program requires the screening date within a defined window (e.g., on or after January 1 of the current year). November 14 would almost certainly fall inside any such window.
4. Results must be recorded on the attestation form itself in the specified units, not attached as a lab printout. Some forms require the actual values, not a "normal/abnormal" checkbox.

How to settle it: the attestation form you plan to print will list the exact required fields. Compare that list against what Dr. Chen's office plans to order. If the form requires anything outside her routine panel (waist, A1c, cotinine), ask the office in advance to add it on November 14 so a second visit is not needed.

Next action: paste Section 4.3 here or read it alongside the attestation form's field list; then call Dr. Chen's office with the specific list of measurements and labs the form requires and confirm all can be done at the November 14 visit, fasting if the lipid panel or glucose requires it.

yeah that's fair, you don't have section 4.3 in front of you. i'll pull it up after lunch and compare with the attestation form. but just to make sure i'm not missing something obvious—the form itself should list exactly what they need, right? like if it says "waist circumference" and dr. chen doesn't normally do that, i'd need to ask ahead of time.

Yes on both points, with one qualifier on the first.

The form should list exactly what they need. In most programs the attestation form is the operative definition of "qualified biometric screening": if a field is on the form, it is required; if the form is missing a value the program wants, the submission is rejected or held. Two exceptions to check: some forms mark certain fields optional (read the fine print or footnotes), and some programs also state requirements in the handbook (your Section 4.3) that the form does not repeat, such as a screening-date window or fasting requirement. So treat the form as the primary list and Section 4.3 as a cross-check.

If the form lists something outside Dr. Chen's routine physical, you need to ask ahead. Waist circumference is the common example: it takes 30 seconds but is often skipped unless requested. Same applies to A1c versus fasting glucose, or a cotinine test. Asking before the visit avoids a second appointment, which matters because a return visit after November 14 leaves little room before December 1.

Next action: after lunch, print the form, read every field including footnotes, compare against Section 4.3, then call Dr. Chen's office with the list and confirm each item can be done on November 14.

hmm actually, while i'm thinking about it—section 4.5 says something about when the credit actually shows up. "discount application starting january 1" is what 4.2 says, but does that mean it's on the first january paycheck or does it take a cycle to kick in? like if the attestation form lands on december 1, is the jan 1 start date real or is there some lag?

I do not have Section 4.5's text, so I cannot tell you what your plan does; paste it and I can read it. Section 4.2's phrase "discount application starting January 1" establishes an effective date, not a paycheck date, and those two often differ.

What "starting January 1" typically means, stated as inference from common payroll and benefits practice:
- The premium discount applies to coverage periods beginning January 1. It appears on whichever paycheck first deducts January premiums. If your employer deducts premiums in advance, that can be a late-December check; if in arrears, it is a January or early-February check.
- Programs commonly set a processing cutoff 2–4 weeks before the effective date. A December 1 submission deadline with a January 1 effective date is consistent with that: it gives the vendor roughly four weeks to verify forms and send eligibility files to payroll.
- Forms submitted near the deadline are at higher risk of missing the first payroll file. Programs handle that in one of two ways: retroactive credit applied as a lump-sum adjustment on a later check, or the discount starting the next pay period with no back-payment. Which one your plan uses is the thing to find in 4.5.

Unknowns, each material to whether "January 1 is real" for you:
1. Whether your employer deducts premiums in advance or in arrears. Check: your current pay stub's premium deduction versus the coverage period shown.
2. Whether 4.5 promises retroactive adjustment for late-verified submissions. Check: look for the words "retroactive," "adjustment," or "next available pay period" in 4.5.
3. Whether the December 1 date is "received by" or "postmarked." Check: attestation form instructions.
4. Whether the form goes through the benefits team or a third-party wellness vendor, which adds a transfer step. Check: the form's return address or upload portal.

Practical implication: a submission landing on December 1 is inside the rule but at the edge of the processing window. Submitting by about November 20 reduces the chance the credit slips to the second January check or later, regardless of what 4.5 says about retroactivity.

Next action: paste Section 4.5 here after lunch; separately, check one current pay stub to determine whether premiums are deducted in advance or arrears, since that alone determines which check would first show a January 1 discount.
